lines.text: A whole city, sealed under the streets. A tomb covered in thousands of wishes. A prison its own inmates built, then burned. And a hotel where a fake doctor sold a cure that didn't exist. Four places hiding in plain sight, partner. Come on.
June 6, 1889. A pot of glue tipped over in a carpentry shop. The Great Seattle Fire burned the heart of the city.
Old Seattle sat on soggy tideflats. At high tide, toilets could erupt.
So when they rebuilt, they raised the streets one to two stories higher. The old storefronts and sidewalks were sealed in underneath.
Glass tiles in the new sidewalks let a little daylight down into the dark.
In 1907 the city condemned the underground, afraid of bubonic plague. For decades, it was left to rot.
In 1965 a local author, Bill Speidel, started tours. You can still walk it today.
New Orleans. Saint Louis Cemetery Number One, founded in 1789. The oldest cemetery still standing in the city.
The dead here rest above ground, in tombs of brick and plaster.
One tomb is believed to hold Marie Laveau, the city's famous voodoo priestess. She died in 1881.
The legend. Mark her tomb with three X's, make a wish... and she'll grant it.
Thousands did. Marker. Lipstick. Scratches in the stone. People left coins, flowers and gifts in the cracks.
Then someone painted her whole tomb pink. Since 2015, you can only go inside with a registered tour guide.
Boise, Idaho. The Old Idaho Penitentiary took its first prisoners in 1872.
Inmates quarried the sandstone, and built its walls themselves.
Over a hundred and one years, more than thirteen thousand people were locked up here. About two hundred and fifteen of them were women. Ten men were executed here.
Its most notorious inmate, Harry Orchard, killed a former governor with a bomb. He died inside, in 1954.
In 1971 and 1973, inmates rioted over conditions, and set buildings on fire. It closed in December 1973. The burned walls are still standing.
Today it's a museum. Ghost hunting shows have filmed inside.
Eureka Springs, Arkansas. The Crescent Hotel opened in 1886. A luxury resort in the Ozark mountains.
Legend says an Irish stonemason called Michael fell to his death while it was being built.
1937. Norman Baker bought it. He had no medical license. He opened the Baker Cancer Hospital.
He promised a cure without surgery. Desperate patients came from all over the country. There was no cure. In 1940, Baker went to federal prison, for mail fraud.
The basement he used as a morgue is still there.
Today it's a hotel again, with nightly ghost tours. Staff say Michael's favorite room is two eighteen.

Four places. A buried city, a wishing tomb, a burned prison, and a hotel that sold false hope. Which one would you check into tonight? Tell me in the comments. Subscribe for more files. I'll be waiting, partner.
